question: In GPU deep learning, why can the numerical values inside dense matrices change matrix multiplication speed?
guest: Matmuls actually avoid a lot of the usual ways data impacts performance: they have identical memory access patterns regardless of what data is in your tensor, there is no control flow in the matmul, and GPUs don't have denormal slowdowns. Yet if you benchmark tensors initialized with all zeros, a Gaussian distribution, and a uniform distribution, you find a real performance difference depending on the data. The actual cause is dynamic or switching power. When a GPU is under load, it uses more power and eventually throttles at its power or heat limit. That power largely comes from switching power: every time a transistor on the GPU flips from zero to one or one to zero, it dissipates a little power, so total power usage sums across all transistor switching. If you multiply with all zeros, or if your model NaNs so every tensor is NaN, many transistors never flip at all. As a result, the GPU consumes less power, throttles much less, and delivers measurably faster performance.

points.core: GPU dynamic power rises with the total number of transistor bit transitions.
points.note: Accept: switching power, CMOS bit flips, or toggling circuits between zero and one consuming energy. Do not credit: generic claims that GPUs consume power without linking power draw to bit transitions.

points.note: Accept: all-zeros, all-NaNs, sparse, or constant values reducing switching activity compared to random floats. Do not credit: claiming dense matmuls skip zero multiplications via control flow or sparsity.

The algorithm does the same number of operations regardless of the values; the speed difference comes from power and heat, not from the maths. This is from memory (I didn't search), chiefly Horace He's write-up on "predictable" data making GPU matmuls faster.

A GPU's dynamic power draw depends on how many transistors switch state each cycle. Multiplying matrices of all zeros, or of repeated or otherwise low-entropy values, causes few bit flips in the multipliers, adders, registers and memory buses, so the chip uses less power. Random, high-entropy values toggle many more bits, so power draw and heat rise.

Modern GPUs run near their power and thermal limits. When the workload draws more power, the GPU lowers its clock frequency to stay within those limits, and the same matmul takes longer. Predictable data keeps the chip cooler, lets it hold a higher clock, and so finishes faster.

It follows that benchmarks using zeros or constant tensors can overstate real-world speed, so use realistic random data.

A separate CPU-side effect is that denormal floating-point values can trigger slow handling paths.

models.answer: Although dense matrix multiplication executes a fixed instruction sequence and takes essentially the same number of clock cycles regardless of operand values, those values alter physical hardware behavior—primarily power draw and clock frequency. In CMOS chips, dynamic power consumption scales with transistor switching activity. High-entropy random numbers cause frequent bit flips across buses, registers, and Tensor Core datapaths, drawing substantially more power than zeros, constants, or structured values that keep signals steady. When intense switching pushes the GPU against its power, current, or thermal limits, dynamic boost controllers throttle clock frequencies downward to stay within budget, making the exact same cycle count take longer in wall-clock time. Two secondary hardware effects can also play a role: modern GPUs apply transparent lossless compression to memory traffic, increasing effective bandwidth for zeros or repetitive bit patterns in memory-bound regimes, and subnormal numbers (when not flushed to zero) or special IEEE values like NaNs can trigger slower floating-point execution paths on certain pipelines.

noweb.answer: Even though dense matrix multiplication executes the exact same instructions regardless of input data, the numerical values physically alter GPU hardware behavior, primarily through power-driven clock throttling and memory compression. Dynamic power draw in silicon depends directly on transistor switching activity. Multiplying matrices filled with zeros or repeated constants causes minimal bit-flipping, consuming far less energy than high-entropy random floats that constantly toggle bits across data buses and Tensor Cores. When dense random values push a GPU against its power or thermal limits, dynamic frequency scaling throttles clock speeds downward, making real-world weights run noticeably slower than zero-initialized benchmarks. Additionally, modern GPUs apply transparent, lossless hardware compression to cache lines moving between HBM and on-chip caches; zero-heavy or low-variance values compress efficiently, conserving memory bandwidth and accelerating bandwidth-sensitive operations. Finally, in floating-point pipelines where flush-to-zero is disabled, special IEEE values such as subnormals, NaNs, or infinities can trigger slower microarchitectural handling paths, further tying execution speed to the specific numbers inside the matrices.

Values change matmul speed because modern GPUs are usually limited by power, not just by how much arithmetic they can do. The arithmetic logic is the same whatever the data, but the energy it uses is not. Dynamic power in CMOS circuits comes from transistors switching between 0 and 1. When tensor cores multiply random, high-entropy numbers, many bits flip on every cycle in the multipliers, adders, registers and data paths. When the inputs are all zeros, constants, or very regular patterns, far fewer bits toggle, so each operation uses less energy.

Large GEMMs drive the chip close to its power limit (TDP). Once it hits that limit, the GPU lowers its clock speed to stay within budget. Data that draws more power therefore causes more throttling and lower measured throughput. Horace He showed this on A100/H100-class GPUs, where all-zero or predictable matrices ran noticeably faster than normally distributed random ones. Sparse-looking values, low-entropy bit patterns, and even the sign and magnitude distribution all affect it.

So benchmark matmuls with realistic data and watch clocks and power, or you'll overestimate the FLOPS you'll actually get.

noweb.answer:
A standard dense GPU matrix multiply performs the same operations for a given shape, data type, and kernel. It multiplies by zero just as it multiplies by any other value, so adding zeros to a dense matrix usually leaves the runtime unchanged.

Values can affect speed when the hardware or software treats some data differently. A sparsity-aware kernel can skip zeros if the matrix is stored in a supported sparse format. On GPUs with lossless memory compression, compressible patterns can reduce the amount of data moved and speed up a memory-bound multiply. Very small floating-point values called subnormals can also be slower on some hardware paths, depending on the precision and whether the hardware flushes them to zero.

models.answer:
For a standard dense GPU matrix multiplication, the matrix shapes and data type determine how many multiply-adds the GPU performs. A zero usually costs the same instruction as any other value. But the values can still affect how fast those instructions run: moving and multiplying successive operands with different bit patterns can make more transistors switch, increasing power draw. If the GPU reaches its power or thermal limit, it can lower its clock speed, so the same instruction sequence takes longer.

That’s why a benchmark using all zeros or repeated values can run faster than one using random values, even when both use exactly the same dense kernel. If the GPU sustains the same clock in both cases, the timing difference from this effect should largely disappear.
